segments: This is Törus: a protocol on Solana that makes a company's promise to give back to its customers checkable, and makes lying cost more than it gains. Everything you see is a real program running on a local Solana validator.

Scene one. The rules are locked in when the token is registered. A token the company could still freeze is rejected. ACME registers with a one percent transfer fee and the Törus transfer hook, and the authority to change the fee or the hook is revoked. Collected fees can only be withdrawn by a program address that has no private key. The company can't appoint itself as the auditor, and it can't set its own bond. The operator does.

Scene two. Every trade pays one percent, withheld by Token twenty twenty-two, and the hook counts the volume. The company can't withdraw these fees, but anyone can sweep them into a program-owned vault. No promises are accepted until the bond is full. A registered exchange partner buys the fees for USDC. The operator's share goes to its treasury, and the company's share fills the slashing bond first. Now the next period's fees fill the redemption pool, and when the period closes on a fixed boundary, the program computes the obligation from the trading volume. The company never reports it.

Scene three. The company commits a Merkle-sum root of the payments it made to merchants. Only the root goes on chain. The program checks that every payment ID is unique, so nothing can be counted twice. After the commit, a random sample is drawn, from a verifiable random function in production. The company discloses those payments with proofs, and an independent auditor records what the payment processor actually saw. The audit passes. Anyone can submit a claim, but the money only goes to the merchant in the committed ledger, and only once. Payments outside the sample are paid after the auditor confirms them.

Scene four. BRAVO claims a thousand dollars of returns it never delivered. The sampled payments come back at ten percent. The program counts the defects, slashes the entire bond into the compensation pool, resets the tier, and freezes the token. Trading stops.

Scene five. No escape hatches. CHARLIE lists the same payment twice, and the uniqueness check rejects it. It can't move on to the next period while the audit is open, and nobody can call the deadline early. Then CHARLIE goes silent. Once the deadline passes, any customer can declare the default, and the bond is slashed, just as if it had lied.

Scene six. DELTA honestly reports eight hundred dollars against a one thousand dollar obligation. An honest shortfall is not slashed, and the token keeps trading. DELTA loses a tier, and the missing two hundred dollars is added to the next period's obligation, so under-reporting never makes a promise disappear. What gets punished is claiming more than was delivered.

Every outcome here was decided by the program, not by a person. In this demo, the auditor's observations are entered by hand and the USDC is a test token. Next, we connect payment processors so that returns can be traced end to end. Törus. Patent pending.
